extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, development practitioners, and journalists interested in media coverage of climate change and adaptation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and interpreting how mass media report on climate change and adaptation — patterns of coverage, drivers and barriers, effects on public understanding, and the roles of claims-makers across countries and media platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-driven spikes in coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Media coverage of climate change and adaptation increases during major events (e.g., IPCC assessment reports in 1990, 1995, 2001; UN FCCC 1992; Kyoto Protocol 1997).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use searches for keywords around such events to detect increases; interpret coverage trends as partially agenda-driven by high-profile scientific and policy events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic disparity in coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage outside Europe and North America is considerably lower; much coverage in non-Western outlets is repurposed material from Western newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing global media attention, account for reliance on republished Western sources and notably reduced local reporting in many developing-country outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low levels of knowledge among journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: A barrier to coverage: journalists and editors have low levels of knowledge about climate change and adaptation linked to a lack of access to timely, clear and understandable information and excessive jargon from scientists/NGOs/institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider journalists' access to clear information and the role of jargon; improving clarity and timeliness of information can increase coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient financial resources for reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: A barrier: limited financial resources constrain first-hand reporting and the allocation of time to environmental 'beats'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsroom resource constraints (staffing, travel, dedicated beats) as a structural factor limiting depth and frequency of adaptation coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruent journalistic habits and priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: A barrier: newsrooms prioritize crime and violence stories that 'sell', leading editors and advertisers to prefer dramatic stories over environmental/ adaptation reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider editorial incentives and commercial pressures when judging why adaptation stories are under-reported; audience- and advertiser-driven priorities shape news agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition of issues for public attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate news stories (mitigation and adaptation) compete with many other public issues for media attention and public engagement (Downs’ Issue Attention Cycle; Hilgartner & Bosk’s Public Arenas Model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply issue-attention frameworks to explain waxing and waning coverage; expect episodic attention and competition with more immediate concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural disadvantage of poorer nations in preparedness and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Poorer and vulnerable countries are at a structural disadvantage in preparing for and responding to disasters; weak media institutions and colonial legacies exacerbate reduced coverage and capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret low media attention alongside socio-economic/institutional vulnerability; reduced coverage may worsen adaptive outcomes by limiting discussion and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign correspondent dominance and mediated local interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: International/foreign correspondents often dominate coverage in some countries, mediating local interpretations and prioritizing immediate, on-the-spot reporting over long-term or contextual analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether coverage foregrounds short-term spectacle (live TV/radio) versus contextual reporting; reliance on foreign correspondents can marginalize local perspectives and long-term adaptation debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phases/waves of public engagement with science
rubrics_metrics.description: Three waves described: 1) deficit model (lack of knowledge is root cause), 2) democracy (call for upstream engagement and non-state actor participation), 3) normative theory of expertise (delineating authorized experts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these conceptual waves to assess communication strategies: merely supplying information (deficit) is insufficient; inclusion and clear roles for expertise are important for engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and amplification of scientific uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass media often amplify scientific uncertainty (e.g., by featuring contrarian counter-claims) and may construct uncertainty as a boundary between the public and scientists, fostering calls for 'more research' and inaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether reporting contextualizes uncertainty and clarifies consensus vs. marginalized views; look for translation of technical uncertainty into meaningful analogies for lay audiences ('translating error bars into ordinary language').

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualization mitigates controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental evidence (three newspaper story treatments: controversy, context, control) shows that greater contextualization in climate stories helps mitigate controversy stirred by uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize contextual framing (historical, scientific consensus, implications) in reporting to reduce the impact of contrarian controversy on reader perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge increases action only with supporting beliefs/attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Increases in knowledge raise stated intentions to act only if existence beliefs, attitudes, and beliefs about responsibility are in place to allow reasoning steps to unfold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate communication not just on factual accuracy but on whether it connects to audiences' pre-existing beliefs and norms that enable action; single-message knowledge campaigns may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messages to audience values and predispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages about climate change need to be tailored to particular audiences — sometimes challenging misconceptions directly, other times resonating with strongly held values (egalitarian vs hierarchical, individual vs communal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences and adapt framing and appeals (values-based messaging) rather than using a 'one-size-fits-all' scientific-information approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral preferences: mitigation favored over adaptation; in-group bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological studies show preference for mitigation measures over adaptation and for helping people in one's own country before others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communications and policy advocacy with awareness of these preferences; emphasize locally relevant adaptation benefits where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary media channels for public science information
rubrics_metrics.description: Television is the primary source of information, the internet is secondary; many internet users encounter science news while using the web for other reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess outreach strategies across TV and online platforms; use internet channels both as direct science outlets and as incidental discovery points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox of specialized knowledge and compartmentalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater specialization can lead to compartmentalized groups of understanding; bridging metaphors can be inappropriate or misapplied, leaving the public concerned but ill-informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious employing metaphors; tailor communication to avoid misapplication and address compartmentalized understandings across audience groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey/poll limitations and interpretation cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Large international polls (e.g., Nielsen) are informative but limited by varying acquiescence, cultural interpretations of terms (e.g., 'global warming'), and socio-economic/educational biases among internet users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret survey results with caveats; adjust conclusions for cultural and demographic sampling differences and measurement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims-makers and power in framing debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-state actors (contrarians, NGOs, think tanks, industry) have significant discursive traction; those with power to define terms of debate strongly influence outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media discourse, identify dominant claims-makers, their networks (e.g., ties between contrarians and conservative think tanks), and how they shape public understanding and policy debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrarian tactics and common counter-claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrarians commonly deploy three counter-claims: 1) the evidentiary basis of global warming is weak/uncertain/flawed; 2) global warming will have substantial benefits; 3) climate policy will do more harm than good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot and contextualize these claims in coverage; trace connections to organized opposition (think tanks, anti-environment movements, carbon-based industry) and juxtapose with scientific consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: NGO engagement: reliance on scientific authority and contextual limits
rubrics_metrics.description: NGOs rely on scientific authority to make claims, but expertise built around one boundary does not automatically transfer to another — many challenges are contextual rather than purely strategic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate NGO media strategies for appropriate use of scientific authority and for understanding contextual limits when transferring expertise across policy/science boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerns about 'catastrophism' or 'alarmism' in NGO/scientific framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scholars and practitioners warn that framing climate change as 'catastrophic' (and using qualifiers like 'chaotic', 'irreversible', 'rapid') can alter public discourse and may push beyond what science can claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the balance between drawing urgent attention and overstating claims; consider potential backlash or credibility loss from alarmist framings.
